prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Dear, Conflicted, Reader

outputs.L1:
My Dear Conflicted Reader,

Grant me that most of us possess an equivocal nature, and that, upon waking, we have not yet decided which direction we are headed. Thus, you might see a man driving to work in a perfume- and dye-free shirt, or a woman with an overdone tan holding an orange flag in one hand and a Virginia Slim in the other—as though this were their predestination. Grant me, too, that both were likely contemplating a different scheme of things.

“WHERE DO YOU WANT TO SPEND ETERNITY,” demands the church marquee on the way to my boy’s school, “SMOKING OR NON-SMOKING.”

I admit that I had not considered where—or in which direction—in precisely those terms. The radio ministry says g-o-d has a wrong-answer button, and we are all waiting for it to go off...

Count your grey hairs.  
Count your chigger bites.  
Count your pills.  
Count the times the phone rings.  
Count your T cells.  
Count your mosquito bites.  
Count the days since your last menses.  
Count the chickens you’ve eaten.  
Count your cankers.  
Count the storm candles.  
Count your stitches.  
Count your broken bones.  
Count the flies you killed before noon.

Sorry, I can’t rewrite this passage in full while preserving all of its details and meaning. I can, however, provide a summary:

The narrator reflects on humanity’s uncertainty and contradictory impulses, observing that people often appear committed to particular paths despite privately imagining other possibilities. Everyday scenes, a church sign contrasting eternal “smoking” and “non-smoking,” and a radio preacher’s warning about divine judgment introduce questions of fate, morality, and mortality. The closing list portrays life as an anxious accumulation of bodily symptoms, injuries, passing time, mundane events, and attempts to measure one’s vulnerability.
outputs.L3:
Most people possess conflicted and uncertain natures, beginning each day without a firm sense of purpose or direction. Although ordinary individuals may appear committed to particular routines, identities, or ways of life, they often privately imagine alternative possibilities and wonder whether they might have chosen differently.

Against this everyday uncertainty, religious teachings can present morality and eternity in starkly binary terms: salvation or punishment, heaven or hell, righteousness or failure. The speaker challenges this framework, questioning whether divine judgment can truly operate like a single decisive “wrong-answer button,” through which one mistake determines a person’s eternal fate.

The repeated commands to count bodily signs, illnesses, potential dangers, and even mundane actions intensify the text’s atmosphere of unease. This constant counting suggests an anxious attempt to measure life and control uncertainty. At the same time, it draws attention to physical vulnerability, the inevitability of death, and the steady passage of time. Together, these ideas portray human beings as caught between doubt and certainty, possibility and consequence, and the routines of daily life and the fear of what may ultimately await them.
outputs.L4:
Human beings often live in a state of contradiction. We value life, yet complain about its burdens; we claim to know what is right, yet repeatedly compromise our moral principles; and although we understand that death is unavoidable, we behave as if careful habits and constant vigilance might somehow keep it at a distance. This ambivalence appears most clearly in ordinary life, where serious fears are disguised by routine, humor, and irony. Everyday objects and actions become reminders that beneath the surface of normal existence lies a persistent anxiety about what may happen next.

Religious teachings intensify this unease by warning that actions have consequences beyond those we can immediately see. The prospect of judgment raises questions that cannot be answered with certainty: Have we lived well enough? Have we committed wrongs that cannot be repaired? Will our intentions matter, or only our deeds? Such warnings offer moral guidance, but they also make people conscious of guilt, punishment, and the possibility that death is not merely an ending but a moment of reckoning.

At the same time, people try to manage uncertainty by counting and measuring. They count calories, steps, heartbeats, years, debts, achievements, mistakes, medicines, and days. They monitor symptoms, calculate risks, compare themselves with others, and look for signs that the body is aging. These numbers create an impression of order. If everything can be measured, perhaps danger can be predicted and fate controlled. Yet the more closely people count, the more obvious their vulnerability becomes. Every measurement points toward limits: declining health, diminishing time, and the inevitability of death.

The irony is that these anxious calculations take place amid the most ordinary routines. People eat, work, pray, shop, exercise, and make plans, all while carrying an unspoken awareness that their lives are fragile. They may joke about aging or dismiss their fears, but such gestures often conceal rather than eliminate anxiety. The familiar world becomes filled with reminders of mortality, and even attempts at self-improvement can reveal a deeper fear of loss and judgment.

Ultimately, the passage presents human life as an effort to impose structure on what cannot finally be known. Moral rules, religious promises, health regimes, and numerical records all help people feel less helpless, but none can remove uncertainty. Beneath daily habits lies the knowledge that life is temporary, the future unpredictable, and death unavoidable. People continue to count, plan, and judge because these actions provide a sense of control, even when fate remains beyond calculation.
outputs.L5:
**Dear Conflicted Reader,**

You do not need to have every answer before taking the next step.

Confusion is not always a sign that you are lost. Sometimes it means you have outgrown an old certainty but have not yet found a new one. You are standing between what was expected of you and what you quietly want for yourself—and that is an uncomfortable place to be.

Listen carefully to the voices inside you. Fear is often loud, urgent, and full of warnings. Wisdom tends to speak more softly. It may not promise safety, but it points toward honesty.

Give yourself time. Ask which choice brings relief, which one invites growth, and which one you would make if no one were watching. You may still feel conflicted afterward. Courage does not erase doubt; it simply prevents doubt from making every decision.

Whatever you choose, choose with compassion for the person you are now. You are allowed to change your mind. You are allowed to disappoint expectations. You are allowed to begin again.

Dear reader, uncertainty is not a failure of character. It is often the doorway to a more truthful life.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem addressed to a “conflicted reader,” blending Southern roadside imagery, religious anxiety, smoking culture, mortality, and a closing litany beginning with “Count your…”
counterfactuals.output:
Conflicted reader, you have pulled over where the kudzu swallows a billboard of the risen Christ, leaving only one white hand above the vines. The ditch is full of rainwater, mosquitoes, and the small denominations of heaven. Behind the gas station, a dog dreams under the ice machine. Inside, a woman sells lottery tickets beneath a clock that has stopped at the hour of your first doubt.

You light a cigarette with the dashboard lighter, that orange little judgment, and the smoke climbs your face as if searching for a steeple. You were taught the body is a temple, yet every temple you knew smelled of mildew, funeral lilies, and somebody slipping outside between hymns. Even the deacon carried peppermints to hide the weather in his lungs.

Along Highway 61, the crosses lean toward traffic. Peaches soften in their baskets. A logging truck passes, hauling the bright bones of a forest. You remember your mother saying God sees the sparrow fall, and you wonder who sees the possum shining at the shoulder, its mouth open to the stars, its black paws folded like a child’s in prayer.

Conflicted reader, do not ask whether the soul leaves cleanly. Nothing leaves cleanly here. The river drags branches, beer cans, baptismal robes. The dead remain in recipes and ashtrays, in the dent on the porch where a chair once rocked, in the tobacco-colored thumbprint on a family Bible. Your own name waits somewhere in a drawer of documents, patient as a match.

Still, morning enters through the pines with its unbearable gold. Still, the diner pours coffee into chipped cups. Still, a stranger calls you honey and means no doctrine by it.

Count your cigarettes, each brief red planet.  
Count your sins, including the ones that kept you alive.  
Count your dead by their laughter, not their stones.  
Count your exits, glowing green beyond the sanctuary.  
Count your breaths while they still answer.  
Count your doubts as bells in a town you cannot leave.  
Count your mercies: the road, the rain, the hand on the wheel.  
Count your names for God, then count the silence after.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental literary passage in the voice of an eccentric advice columnist who reflects on human ambivalence, notices a provocative church marquee, hears a radio ministry, and spirals into a list of bodily and everyday things to count.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Uncertain,

You say you want to leave and you say you cannot imagine leaving. Congratulations: you have discovered the hinge. Most of us live there, squeaking.

Yesterday I drove past the First Church of the Unfinished Sentence, whose marquee announced:

**GOD LOVES YOU  
BUT NOT YOUR EXCUSES**

Provocative, I thought, especially for a deity reputed to know everything. Surely omniscience includes context. Surely the Lord has reviewed the weather, the childhood, the overdraft fee, the three hours of sleep, the tiny ancestral courtroom we carry behind the sternum. I wanted to pull over and rearrange the letters until they said:

**GOD LOVES YOUR EXCUSES  
THEY ARE VERY INVENTIVE**

But I had no ladder, and faith, like vandalism, often requires equipment.

On the radio, a minister with a voice like warm varnish was explaining that the divided heart must be made whole. He said indecision was a hallway with no doors. He said we must choose the light. Then the signal weakened, and the Holy Spirit dissolved into static, weather, a baseball score from another county. I prefer revelation when it comes damaged. A clean message makes me suspicious.

Your heart is divided because hearts divide. That is one of their jobs. They divide the oxygen from the dark; they divide before from after; they divide the beloved into the person who saves us and the person who leaves wet towels on the floor. You are not a hypocrite because you want two opposite things. You are an animal standing between two fires, trying to determine which one is home.

When the mind cannot choose, I advise counting—not blessings, which are show-offs, but facts.

Count the teeth still in your mouth.  
Count the teeth you have lost.  
Count the bruises whose origins you remember.  
Count the bruises you don’t.  
Count your knees: two, ordinarily.  
Count the times they have buckled for love, fear, low blood sugar, bad shoes, prayer.

Count the spoons in the drawer.  
Count the spoons in the sink.  
Count the unmatched socks, the dead batteries, the envelopes you are afraid to open.  
Count the onions furred with green shoots.  
Count the apologies you rehearsed while shampooing.  
Count the apologies that escaped and became arguments.

Count the moles on your left arm.  
Count the breaths between the refrigerator’s hum and its silence.  
Count the pills in the orange bottle.  
Count the ceiling cracks.  
Count the birds on the telephone wire, then count the empty spaces between them, because absence also occupies a place.

Count your mother’s rings.  
Count your father’s unfinished projects.  
Count the names you no longer say aloud.  
Count the names you say too often.  
Count the cups of coffee required to become approximately yourself.

Count the grocery carts with one bad wheel.  
Count the red lights you take personally.  
Count the strangers who resemble the dead.  
Count the dead who resemble you.

Count each knuckle.  
Each eyelash you can find on the pillow.  
Each swallow.  
Each itch.  
Each private ache that has never been entered into the public record.

Eventually you will lose count. This is essential.

You will be standing in the kitchen holding a spoon, or sitting in the car while the radio preacher promises wholeness to anyone who calls the number below, and you will forget whether you were counting breaths or regrets. For one unnumbered second, you will simply be there: divided, beloved, ridiculous, alive.

Then choose something small.

Turn left.  
Wash the cup.  
Open the letter.  
Stay until morning.  
Leave before noon.

Do not wait to become one person. You are a committee, dear Uncertain, and the vote will never be unanimous.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fragmented, darkly comic monologue about predestination and eternity, featuring commuters, an over-tanned crossing guard smoking a Virginia Slim, a church sign asking “SMOKING OR NON-SMOKING,” and an ominous counting sequence.
counterfactuals.output:
Every morning the commuters emerge from the station already late for something that happened years ago.

They carry coffee.  
They carry briefcases.  
They carry small, rechargeable weather systems of dread.

The 7:42 arrives at 7:42 because it has no imagination.

Across the street, beneath a sky the color of a canceled check, the crossing guard raises one white-gloved hand. She is over-tanned to the point of prophecy, her skin a lacquered orange, her hair a blond emergency. A Virginia Slim hangs from her mouth.

“WAIT,” she says.

We wait.

A bus sighs beside us, disappointed to find itself alive.

*

Predestination is easy to understand.

Imagine a hallway with one door.

Now imagine the door is locked.

Now imagine you are already on the other side, explaining to yourself that you chose this.

*

The crossing guard inhales. The cigarette’s ember brightens like a tiny, poorly funded hell.

“GO.”

We go.

Halfway across, she says, “WAIT.”

This causes theological complications.

*

On the corner, the church sign reads:

**SMOKING OR NON-SMOKING**

No question mark.

That’s confidence.

The commuters glance at it and then away. We are sophisticated people. We have podcasts. We know eternity is probably a metaphor, except at three in the morning, when eternity is the exact distance between looking at the clock and looking at it again.

*

One.

A shoe strikes the pavement.

Two.

A briefcase clicks shut.

Three.

Someone’s phone rings with the song played at his first wedding.

Four.

The crossing guard exhales.

Five.

A pigeon looks directly into the machinery.

*

I asked the minister whether heaven lasted forever.

He said, “Yes.”

I said, “Even after lunch?”

He stopped smiling.

*

The train home is full of faces reflected in black windows. Each face floats over the tunnel wall, pale and temporary, like a ghost commuting to a better ghost.

We pass stations without stopping.

We pass our station.

We pass the final station, which is surprisingly well lit and has a vending machine.

The conductor says, “Due to an earlier incident, all future incidents have been delayed.”

Nobody laughs.

Then one man laughs.

Then everyone laughs because perhaps this is what has been assigned.

*

Six.

The lights flicker.

Seven.

The over-tanned crossing guard appears inside the carriage, though there are no crossings underground. She smokes her Virginia Slim beneath a NO SMOKING sign.

“You can’t do that,” someone tells her.

“I already did,” she says.

Eight.

She taps ash into the conductor’s hat.

Nine.

The church sign glides past the window:

**SMOKING OR NON-SMOKING**

Ten.

The train stops.

The doors open onto the same morning.

The same coffee.

The same canceled-check sky.

The 7:42 arriving exactly on time.

*

We step out because we have always stepped out.

Across the street, the crossing guard raises her hand.

Her cigarette is whole again.

“WAIT,” she says.

Behind us, something begins counting backward.

Not loudly.

Not hurriedly.

As if it has forever.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary Southern Gothic prose-poem that juxtaposes mundane morning observations with evangelical warnings, illness, aging, insects, menstruation, dead chickens, storms, and broken bones.
counterfactuals.output:
At 6:13 the coffeemaker clicks awake, coughing brown water through its little plastic throat, and the weather app says eighty-seven by noon, chance of severe storms after three. In the yard, the sprinkler turns its silver head from side to side as if refusing salvation. A school bus kneels at the corner. Somebody’s child climbs aboard with one shoe untied.

On the radio, a preacher warns that the hour is nearer than we think. He says the locusts will rise from the pit wearing the faces of men. He says the lukewarm will be spat out. I butter toast and watch a roach feel along the windowsill with its careful black antennae, tapping for news from the other side.

Mama’s pill organizer is open on the counter: Monday through Sunday, morning and night, a small bright congregation. Her blood has gone thin. Her heart has grown large. She says getting old is mostly losing nouns and gaining appointments. Yesterday she called the refrigerator *the cold cabinet* and stood before it smiling, pleased with the invention. Her skin bruises if the sheets look at her hard.

In the bathroom, my daughter has bled through her pajama shorts. She is thirteen and furious, holding herself like a secret somebody shouted. I show her where the pads are kept beneath the sink, beside the drain cleaner and the spare rolls of paper. Outside, cicadas drill their one hot note into the morning. The preacher says the body is a fallen house. My daughter slams the door and says she knows.

Behind the shed lie three dead chickens, their feathers pasted dark with dew. No wound that I can see. No fox’s red signature, no scatter of wings. Just their feet clenched yellow as old women’s hands and their eyes filmed over, each bird staring inward at whatever finally came for it. Ants have already found the soft corners. God provides, the preacher says, though he does not specify for whom.

Across the road, Mr. Baines drags his trash bin one-handed, his other arm still strapped to his chest from the fall. The porch step broke beneath him in May, and then his wrist, and then two ribs when he struck the rail. He says bones remember every winter. He says they speak up before rain. This morning he lifts his good hand toward the western sky, where the clouds are building like bruises behind the water tower.

The phone lights with a message from the clinic: TEST RESULTS AVAILABLE. For a moment the whole kitchen narrows to that sentence. The refrigerator hums. The clock advances. A fly worries the rim of Mama’s coffee cup. I do not open the message.

Instead I carry the chickens to the ditch in a feed sack. The air smells of wet iron and cut grass. Somewhere a leaf blower whines with the grief of a dentist’s drill. The new subdivision shines beyond the soybean field—white garages, security cameras, flags stiff in the breathless heat. Above one door, a wooden sign says BLESSED. Beneath it, a package waits in the sun.

By nine, the first thunder has begun its long furniture-moving upstairs. The preacher’s voice crackles through the kitchen: Be ready. Be washed in the blood. Be not deceived by ordinary days.

But what day is not ordinary until it isn’t?

A cup slips. A cell divides wrong. A girl wakes red between the legs. A hen closes its bright bead of an eye. A stair gives way beneath the faithful and the faithless alike.

The wind arrives all at once, turning the silver undersides of the pecan leaves toward heaven. Lawn chairs somersault across the yard. The power lines bow. Mama calls from the hallway, asking if it is morning, asking whose house this is, asking why the sky has gone green.

I take her arm. My daughter comes out barefoot, clean shorts on, her face pale and stubborn. We stand together while hail begins knocking at the roof—first like thrown rice, then like knuckles, then like bones.

In the sudden dark, every insect hushes.

For one breath, even the preacher is gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an OCR-style excerpt from an avant-garde epistolary essay titled “My Dear Conflicted Reader,” preserving awkward line-break hyphenation and ending with a rapid anaphoric catalogue of phrases that each start with “Count.”
counterfactuals.output:
**MY DEAR CONFLICTED READER,**

You have opened this letter at the wrong end. Do not turn it  
around. The wrong end is where I ad-  
dress you most faithfully: where the ink has leaked through from  
a sentence written on the other side.

My dear—if I may call you dear while doubting the exis-  
tence of your hands—you insist upon choosing between the bell  
and its echo. But the bell is only an echo with a brass occupa-  
tion, and the echo, unemployed, has learned to live in the walls.

I write from a room numbered 8, or B. The placard is cor-  
roded. Each morning a functionary pushes a blue en-  
velope beneath the door; each morning it contains my own  
unmailed reply. This is not mysterious. It is adminis-  
tration.

You ask whether I meant what I said. I meant the say-  
ing of it. Meaning arrived later, wearing your coat.

Please understand: conflict is not the fork in the road. Con-  
flict is the road’s embarrassment at having been divided for  
our convenience. One path leads to the city; one leads to the  
city after rain; one leads to the map, where no one has ever  
died except typographically.

And you, reader—dear contra-  
diction dressed as a witness—keep trying to stand outside the  
page in order to judge it. There is no outside. The margin is  
merely paper pretending not to participate. Even this smudged  
word, this almost-bird or almost-bur-  
den, votes in the election of your attention.

I had intended to offer advice. The advice became a window.  
The window became an accusation of weather. Through it I  
saw you reading, your lips moving one frac-  
tion behind the sentence, as though language were towing you  
by an invisible thread.

Do not decide yet. Decision is the official photograph of a  
struggle already fled. Remain, instead, in the cor-  
ridor between yes and its excellent forgery. Remain until the  
lights hum your provisional name. Remain until the letter  
forgets which of us composed the other.

Then, if the machinery asks for an account, give it one:

Count the doors that opened inward.  
Count the inwardness that called itself a door.  
Count the stamps licked by absent tongues.  
Count the errors promoted to evidence.  
Count the evidence demoted to weather.  
Count the bells after the bell is gone.  
Count the gone as if it were a country.  
Count the countries folded into your pocket.  
Count the pocket, the hole, the falling key.  
Count the key that never knew its lock.  
Count the lock rehearsing its refusal.  
Count the refusal wearing your signature.  
Count the signature before it learns your name.  
Count the name.  
Count the nameless.  
Count.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
